policy_title: Create More Freeports and Business Rates Retention Zones
stated: The Conservative Party will create more Freeports and enable councils to retain all business rates growth within defined zones for 25 years to finance new infrastructure and invest in local industries.

source.quote: Create more Freeports and Business Rates Retention zones. Freeports have already generated just under £3 billion in investment, which in turn will create thousands of jobs. ...We will enable councils to retain all business rates growth within a defined zone for 25 years...

bearing_set.reason: Freeports and business-rates retention zones are explicitly designed to attract inward investment, stimulate local industry, and generate employment — directly affecting job creation, wages, and job quality in targeted areas.

Freeports and 25-year business-rates retention are explicitly designed to attract business investment, build infrastructure, and raise economic productivity and opportunity in designated zones — directly targeting the aggregate prosperity indicators.

These are geographically targeted interventions aimed at economically left-behind areas; the concrete mechanism — concentrating investment in specific low-activity zones — is intended to narrow regional inequality, a named O14 indicator, though the evidence on displacement vs net creation is contested.

Business rates retention for 25 years removes that revenue growth from national redistribution; freeport tax reliefs (employer NI, capital allowances, SDLT) carry a direct exchequer cost — both are concrete mechanisms that widen the funded/unfunded gap in public finances.

membership_note: Three genuine bearings: the policy's designed-for effect on aggregate prosperity (O13), its regional-inequality dimension (O14), and the fiscal cost of foregone revenue and tax reliefs (O12). Effects on job quality (O4) are too indistinct from O13 here; housing and cohesion links are too indirect to clear the non-negligible bar.
